strengths: Clear and well-motivated RICH hypothesis that addresses a specific gap in Zaremba et al. (2025)
Comprehensive experimental design testing across multiple dimensions: models, attack types, budgets, and scaling approaches
Consistent empirical support for the 'rich-get-richer' effect across Sections 4.1-4.4 with appropriate statistical testing
Insightful visualizations (Figure 1 with attention maps) demonstrating how robust models better follow instructions on OOD data
Novel experimental protocols with explicit security specifications and white-box multimodal attacks
Practical guidance for combining train-time and test-time defenses for synergistic benefits
weaknesses: Limited scope: experiments on VLMs only; frontier model results (Table 4) show no significant benefits for Llama and marginal benefits for Qwen, undermining generality claims
Disconnect from original work: uses naive specification repetition rather than reasoning-based scaling, limiting direct comparison and practical applicability

Insufficient mechanistic explanation: invokes compositional generalization without rigorously explaining why base robustness enables instruction-following on OOD data; lacks investigation of representations

Confounded variable in Section 4.3: reducing ε to help non-robust models fundamentally weakens attacks, making it unclear whether benefits derive from compositional generalization or simply weaker attacks
Limited attack strength: PGD runs 100-300 iterations without comparison to stronger adaptive attacks (AutoAttack); unclear if perturbation budgets are sufficiently challenging
Modest novelty: core finding (robust models benefit more from robustness improvements) is expected; incremental contribution relative to established adversarial robustness literature
Missing ablations on prompt formulation sensitivity and alternative inference-compute scaling strategies beyond naive repetition
Frontier model failure: results in Table 4 contradict RICH predictions for large-scale VLMs, raising questions about generalizability

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine limitations of prior work (Zaremba et al. 2025)
Comprehensive experimental design across multiple models, attack types, and inference-compute approaches with proper statistical testing
Insightful interpretability analysis (Figure 1) showing how robust vs non-robust models use instruction-following differently
Demonstrates that lightweight adversarial finetuning can unlock inference-compute benefits without RL-finetuning
Well-executed ablation studies and controls for confounds (e.g., pre-filling responses to isolate specification effects)
weaknesses: Core hypothesis is somewhat tautological: 'inference compute works better on models already robust to adversarial data' lacks depth and novelty
Critical results on frontier models (Tables 3-4) show RICH breaks down—Qwen and Llama show no/negative benefits on adversarial data, yet this is insufficiently investigated
Scope severely limited to small VLMs (7-13B) and vision-only tasks; generalization to text attacks or larger models unclear
Inference-compute scaling relies on naive approaches (prompt repetition, simple CoT) rather than sophisticated reasoning; this design choice limits testing of the core hypothesis

Experiments confound multiple variables (model scale, adversarial training procedures with different ε values); unclear if results support RICH or just reflect obvious monotonic relationship with adversarial training
Practical improvements are modest (Table 1: ~70% relative improvement but small absolute gains; Table 3: ~10% absolute on Attack-Bard)
No theoretical framework or formal analysis of when/why RICH should hold; mechanism understanding remains superficial
Incomplete investigation of why large models fail to exhibit RICH behavior, undermining claims of generality
Attack strength concerns: only 100-300 PGD steps tested; no adaptive attacks specifically designed against specification-based defenses
Missing reproducibility details and no mention of code availability; multiple models/datasets impede verification

strengths: Clear and testable hypothesis (RICH) that addresses a genuine gap in prior work (Zaremba et al. 2025) regarding why inference compute fails for vision attacks

Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple VLMs (LLaVA, FARE-LLaVA, Delta2-LLaVA, Qwen, Llama), attack types (white-box PGD, black-box transfer), and inference-compute methods (explicit specs, naive scaling, CoT)
Insightful visualizations and interpretability analysis (Figure 1 attention maps) showing that robust models follow instructions better and attacks become more interpretable under robustness
Multiple converging lines of evidence from Tables 1-4 and Figures 3-4 consistently supporting the rich-get-richer dynamic across diverse experimental settings
Good reproducibility with detailed prompts, error bars, statistical testing (McNemar's tests), and clear methodology
Practical actionable insights: layering train-time and test-time defenses, and lightweight adversarial finetuning as a scalable path to unlock inference-compute benefits
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: the core insight that 'more robust models follow instructions better on adversarial data' is intuitive; the paper largely confirms an unsurprising hypothesis rather than discovering a surprising one

RICH hypothesis stated informally and vaguely: 'training data better reflects attacked data's components' lacks precise operationalization; unclear what constitutes a 'component' or how to quantify closeness to training distribution

Causal mechanism underexplored: the paper attributes effects to compositional generalization but doesn't rigorously test this against simpler alternatives (e.g., simply better representations in robust models); no direct measurement of compositional generalization

Concerning inconsistency in large-scale model results: Llama-3.2-Vision-90B shows no statistically significant benefit on adversarial Attack-Bard data (p=7.9e-1), while Qwen-2.5-VL-72B does (p=5.6e-4); this contradicts the generality of the RICH and is not adequately explained
Scale limitations: primary focus on small models (~1.5B parameters); large-scale results are inconsistent, undermining claims about broad applicability

Primitive inference-compute scaling: naive repetition of specifications (K times) is unprincipled; minimal CoT; no RL-based reasoning scaling tested; unclear if findings generalize to sophisticated scaling methods

Methodological inconsistencies: different attack budgets across sections (ε=16/255, 64/255); need to adjust ε per-model to see effects (Section 4.3) undermines universality; pre-filling responses is unusual and may not test true specification following
Limited practical impact: main recommendation ('use adversarial training + inference compute') is relatively obvious; lightweight finetuning approach underdeveloped
Sparse engagement with broader adversarial robustness literature; no comparison with other test-time defense mechanisms or alternative explanations for the observed phenomena

Missing ablations: no granular analysis of vision encoding vs. instruction-following contributions, or how different adversarial training types (contrastive pretraining vs. visual instruction tuning) interact

strengths: Well-motivated RICH hypothesis with clear empirical predictions supported by exploratory findings; comprehensive testing across multiple models (various LLaVA variants, large-scale VLMs), attack types (black-box, white-box, gradient-based), and inference-compute methods

Strong empirical validation showing consistent rich-get-richer effects: security specs help only robust models (Table 2), benefits scale with base robustness (Figure 4), and attack-budget reduction enables benefits in less-robust models (Section 4.3), with appropriate statistical testing

Insightful practical contributions: lightweight adversarial finetuning enables inference-compute benefits; Figure 2 demonstrates novel observation that attacks become more interpretable/geometrically meaningful for robust models; demonstrates robustness benefits without extensive RL finetuning

Thorough experimental design with good controls: pre-filling experiments isolate specification effects, random-token controls verify content matters, ablations in appendices test variants, multiple attack budgets validate RICH predictions

Clarifies important gap in prior work: explains why Zaremba et al. (2025)'s reasoning approach fails on vision attacks and provides actionable guidance for synergistic train-time and test-time defense combinations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: RICH hypothesis is relatively straightforward and builds heavily on existing concepts (compositional generalization, adversarial training, security specifications); the proposed mechanism is assumed rather than rigorously demonstrated through direct measurement

Critical limitation on frontier models: large-scale VLMs (Llama-3.2-Vision-90B, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B) show NO significant benefits on adversarial Attack-Bard data (Table 5); frontier model results show o1-v achieves only 61% vs. robust VLMs performing better, severely limiting practical impact

Compositional generalization mechanism not proven: paper relies on compositional generalization as explanatory mechanism but provides no direct evidence, probing experiments, or representation analysis; connection between base robustness and compositional ability is inferred rather than established

Inference-compute scaling is unsophisticated: main approach is naive specification repetition; no comparison with more sophisticated reasoning methods; claim that RL finetuning is unnecessary seems to underutilize reasoning potential; InternVL gains are modest (≈6% improvement)

Mixed results limit confidence: LLaVA-v1.5 shows no significant CoT benefit on adversarial Attack-Bard data (p=4.2e-2); results strongest only for smaller, adversarially-trained models; benefits degrade significantly at high attack budgets, suggesting narrow applicability

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: lacks theoretical analysis of why base robustness enables compositional generalization; no exploration of alternative explanations; no analysis of fundamental limits; insufficient investigation of why large-scale models fail to benefit

Limited experimental scope: primarily vision attacks on VLMs; doesn't evaluate text jailbreaks that motivated Zaremba et al.; specific perturbation budgets tested; small sample sizes in some experiments (2 replicates); model-scale effects not fully disentangled

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing genuine limitations of prior work (Zaremba et al. 2025) on vision attacks
Well-articulated RICH hypothesis providing a testable framework for characterizing inference-compute benefits
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (small and large), attack types (black-box and white-box), and protocols (visual prompt injection, classification)
Insightful visualization of instruction-following via attention maps (Figure 2) showing robust vs. non-robust model behavior
Thorough ablation studies and controls (Tables 6-8) including random pre-fill experiments testing mechanism
Strong reproducibility through detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and experimental variants
weaknesses: Core insight is intuitive and somewhat tautological—'robust models benefit more from inference compute' largely recapitulates what robustness means; lacks novel theoretical understanding

Results fail to scale to large frontier models (Table 5: Llama-3.2-Vision-90B 27.0→27.5% adversarial, not significant; Qwen-2.5-VL-72B 13.0→18.0% with marginal significance p=0.013), undermining practical relevance where inference scaling matters most

Experimental design conflates different inference scaling methods—uses naive prompt repetition and simple CoT rather than RL-tuned reasoning like Zaremba et al. (2025), weakening comparison to prior work

Section 4.3 key claim (RICH holds for less-robust models) requires reducing attack budget ε from 64/255 to 16/255, appearing to shift conditions specifically to demonstrate RICH rather than showing predictions hold across fixed settings

Insufficient mechanism analysis—posits compositional generalization but lacks rigorous testing; alternative explanations (optimization landscape, attention patterns) not ruled out; no probing studies validating component-level understanding improvements

Misses opportunity to directly validate RICH on o1-v (the motivating case from Zaremba et al.) by testing whether adversarial training would improve inference scaling—Figure 5 shows o1-v but doesn't apply RICH framework
Limited scope to vision-language models and adversarial perturbations; generalization to language-only models, semantic attacks, or other domains unclear
No cost-benefit analysis comparing computational expense of reasoning to robustness gains; adversarial training trade-offs (e.g., harm to clean accuracy) not discussed
Concurrent work (Wu et al. 2025) identifies scaling inference compute increases adversarial risk in certain settings; implications inadequately addressed

Statistical rigor issues: many results lack significance tests, some differences fall within error bars (Table 2 FARE model), inconsistent use of p-values; no formal characterization of RICH boundary conditions
Inconsistent patterns across robustness levels—results strongest for medium-robustness FARE models, less clear for high (Delta2) and low (LLaVA), making generalization unclear

strengths: Directly addresses limitations of Zaremba et al. (2025), providing both explanation and practical solution for why reasoning fails on multimodal attacks
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple model scales, attack types, and inference compute approaches with rigorous statistical testing
Novel experimental protocols (Section 4) including controlled confounds, explicit specifications, and token-level ablations that provide new insights beyond existing work
Demonstrates clear rich-get-richer dynamics with convincing evidence (Figure 4, Table 2) that inference-compute benefits correlate with base model robustness
Practical contribution: shows lightweight adversarial finetuning (FARE) unlocks inference-compute benefits for open-source and non-RL-trained models
Well-executed experiments with strong controls (clean vs. random token pre-fills in Table 6) isolating specification-following ability
Clear presentation with insightful visualizations (particularly Figure 2 on attack interpretability)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core insight that base robustness enables better generalization is intuitive and unsurprising; lacks theoretical depth explaining *why* this occurs mechanistically
Scope limitations at scale: primary focus on smaller LLaVA models; larger models (Qwen-72B, Llama-90B) show minimal adversarial benefits (Tables 4-5), limiting practical impact for deployed systems

Inference-compute scaling methodology concern: uses naive specification repetition (K times) rather than true reasoning depth for non-RL-trained models, unclear if findings generalize to actual reasoning scaling

Insufficient theoretical understanding: no formal analysis of when RICH should hold vs. fail; the mechanism connecting adversarial training to specification-following on OOD data not rigorously justified
Limited failure case analysis: why do frontier models show minimal benefits? When does RICH break down? No systematic boundary condition analysis

Experimental design: different models trained with different ε budgets complicates comparisons; Section 4.3 result (smaller ε enables benefits) is somewhat expected from standard generalization theory
Reproducibility concerns: no code/model release mentioned; some models (Delta2LLaVA-v1.5) may not be publicly available; full reproducibility unclear
Attack methodology: PGD attacks on VLM outputs relatively understudied; unclear if attacks are optimal or if log-likelihood minimization is strongest formulation
Practical significance unclear: Attack-Bard improvements are modest (e.g., 56→65.5% for FARE); benefits vs. inference cost trade-off not thoroughly analyzed
Missing analysis: when should practitioners prefer adversarial training vs. inference compute scaling? Trade-offs with clean accuracy not deeply explored
